questions.q: What is a polling-based event listener actually doing under the hood?
options: Opening one persistent connection that the provider pushes data over
Repeatedly calling the provider (effectively eth_getLogs) on a timed interval to check for anything new
Asking the user's wallet to forward new events
Downloading the entire blockchain to search locally
questions.explain: Polling means your code asks on a fixed interval; nothing is pushed to you between polls.

questions.q: What does a WebSocket subscription require that polling doesn't?
options: A `wss://` endpoint and a persistent connection the client must manage
Manual confirmation from the user for every event
A paid node provider plan — free tiers can never use WebSockets
A smart contract deployed specifically for event forwarding
questions.explain: Subscriptions need a WebSocket-capable endpoint (wss://) and keep a long-lived connection open, unlike the stateless request/response of polling over HTTPS.

questions.q: In both ethers.js and viem, what decides whether your event listener polls or subscribes?
options: Whether the contract is verified on Etherscan
The event name you pass to .on() or watchContractEvent
The gas price configured on the client
The transport/provider type — an HTTP provider polls, a WebSocket provider/transport subscribes
questions.explain: The listening call itself (.on()/watchContractEvent) looks the same either way — it's the underlying provider or transport (http vs. webSocket) that determines the mechanism.

questions.q: Why does a WebSocket-based listener need reconnect logic that a polling listener doesn't?
options: Polling listeners cannot run for more than a few seconds
Reconnect logic is only needed for testnets, not mainnet
A dropped WebSocket connection stays dropped until code notices and re-establishes it, while polling just tries again automatically next interval
WebSocket connections never drop, so the logic is purely precautionary
questions.explain: A dropped subscription silently stops receiving events until the code detects the close event and reconnects; a polling loop has no persistent connection to lose.

questions.q: Why is polling often a better fit than a WebSocket subscription inside a serverless function?
options: Serverless functions are physically incapable of making HTTPS requests
Polling requires no code at all, unlike subscriptions
A serverless function typically exits before a pushed event could arrive, while polling can simply run on its own schedule
WebSocket connections are always more expensive than HTTP requests
questions.explain: Serverless functions are short-lived by design, which doesn't suit a long-lived push connection — a scheduled poll fits that execution model much better.
